sources.title: Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town
sources.author: John H. Moore
sources.publisher: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture
sources.annotation: A focused historical reference on related towns, westward movements and Creek relationships. Its compressed account of the 1936 legislation should be read alongside the original constitution’s separate approval and ratification dates. Not a current citizenship or population source.
sources.contentReviewScope: Complete six-paragraph article, bibliography and publication credit; page navigation excluded.

sources.title: Alabama-Coushatta Indians
sources.author: Howard N. Martin
sources.publisher: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas
sources.annotation: Detailed historical synthesis connecting migration, East Texas settlements, land pressures and institutions. Its sweeping cultural generalizations, assimilation framing and dated figures are not adopted here. Martin also wrote the tribe-hosted chief history: overlap is not independent corroboration.
sources.contentReviewScope: Substantive article and bibliography, especially migration, village networks and land-policy passages; no current demographic or officer claims adopted.

sources.title: Public Law 83-627, chapter 831 — termination of federal supervision (1954)
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, GovInfo
sources.annotation: Original enactment, not a statement of present law. Sections link land conveyance, a later proclamation and withdrawal of federal supervision/services, with specified exceptions. Read with the 1987 restoration act. The neighboring Public Law 628 concerns a different subject.
sources.contentReviewScope: 68 Stat.768–769, complete chapter831, sections1–8 and approval date; two-page PDF also contains parts of unrelated laws, excluded from synthesis. Actual PDF text inspected; no implementation proclamation inspected.

sources.title: Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and Alabama and Coushatta Indian Tribes of Texas Restoration Act — Title II
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.publisher: United States Statutes at Large, GovInfo
sources.annotation: Original act’s Alabama-Coushatta title restores federal recognition and the trust relationship and addresses government and reservation matters. Title I concerns a different nation. This historical reading does not determine later amendments, litigation, present gaming rules or individual rights.
sources.contentReviewScope: TitleII, sections201–207 and approval date, 101 Stat.669–672 (PDF4–7); actual PDF text inspected. TitleI is not used as Alabama-Coushatta evidence.

proposedSections.title: Southeastern towns and different westward journeys
proposedSections.text: John H. Moore’s historical reference follows Alabama and Quassarte towns along the Alabama River into French trade relationships and the Creek Confederacy. It describes westward movement in separate groups, including settlements in central Louisiana and Texas, while people who remained with the Creeks underwent forced removal to Indian Territory. These were different community histories, rather than one journey followed by everyone.

proposedSections.title: Villages, rivers and paths in East Texas
proposedSections.text: Howard Martin’s Handbook history describes Alabama settlements along waterways including the Angelina and Neches rivers. Peach Tree, Fenced-In and Cane Island appear as distinct villages connected through trails. The account links hunting, cultivation and travel to the Big Thicket landscape, then follows settler pressure and land disputes. Read its route descriptions as a historian’s reconstruction, with particular family movements still requiring closer archival comparison.

proposedSections.title: What the 1954 termination act changed
proposedSections.text: The 1954 federal act authorized conveyance of tribal land to Texas to hold in trust. It tied termination of the federal trust relationship to conveyance and a subsequent proclamation, and withdrew many federal services while retaining specified school and hospital eligibility. This was a change in federal administration and obligations; it did not end the people’s existence. The enactment and its later implementation should be distinguished: the proclamation has not been inspected for this introduction.

proposedSections.title: Restoring the federal relationship in 1987
proposedSections.text: Title II of the act approved August 18, 1987 restored federal recognition and the trust relationship for the Alabama and Coushatta Indian Tribes of Texas. It treated the two as one tribal unit for federal-law purposes and addressed the council’s powers, constitution and reservation. The act’s separate title for Ysleta del Sur Pueblo should not be applied to Alabama-Coushatta. This primary document explains an important historical change; later legal developments need their own sources.
